rows.speaker: جماعة
rows.claim: Some define game as any wild animal, edible or not; under this view, a forbidden pilgrim who kills a lion owes compensation capped at a sheep's value.
rows.anchor: وجماعة أن الصيد هو ما توحش مأكولا كان أو غير مأكول. فعلى هذا لو قتل المحرم سبعا لا يؤكل لحمه ضمن ولا يجاوز قيمة شاة

rows.speaker: زفر
rows.claim: Zufar says compensation for killing a wild animal is its full value, however great.
rows.anchor: وقال زفر بالغا ما بلغ

rows.speaker: قوم
rows.claim: Others define game as only edible animals; on this definition, the Shafi‘i view imposes no compensation for lions, the five harmful creatures, or wolves.
rows.anchor: وقال قوم الصيد هو ما يؤكل لحمه فعلى هذا لا يجب الضمان في قتل السبع وهو قول الشافعي ولا في قتل الفواسق الخمس ولا الذئب

rows.speaker: أبو حنيفة ومالك
rows.claim: Abu Hanifa and Malik hold that a pilgrim's slaughter of game does not make it lawful to eat; Ibn al-Musayyib and one opinion of al-Hasan agree.
rows.anchor: فمذهب أبي حنيفة ومالك أنه غير مذكى فلا يؤكل لحمه وبه قال ابن المسيب وأحد قولي الحسن

rows.speaker: الشافعي
rows.claim: Al-Shafi‘i holds that a pilgrim's slaughter does ritually slaughter the game; al-Hakam, Amr ibn Dinar, Sufyan, and another opinion of al-Hasan allow a non-pilgrim to eat it.
rows.anchor: ومذهب الشافعي إن ذبح المحرم الصيد ذكاه، وقال الحكم وعمرو بن دينار وسفيان يحل للحلال أكله

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: On the apparent deliberate-only wording, accidental killing—forgetting ihram, misidentifying game, or a deflected shot—requires no compensation; Ibn Jubayr, Tawus, Ata, Salim, Abu Thawr, Dawud, al-Tabari, and others agree.
rows.anchor: وروي ذلك عن ابن عباس وابن جبير وطاوس وعطاء وسالم

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas says expiation applies only to deliberate killing; they made accidental cases severe so offenders would not repeat them.
rows.anchor: إنما التكفير في العمد وإنما غلظوا في الخطأ لئلا يعودوا

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: One explanation is that deliberate killing is the usual case, so the ruling also covers the rarer accidental case.
rows.anchor: قيل خرج مخرج الغالب فألحق به النادر

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: Another explanation is that the verse mentions deliberation because its occasion was Abu al-Yusr, who deliberately killed a wild donkey while in ihram.
rows.anchor: وقيل ذكر التعمد لأن مورد الآية في من تعمد لقصة أبي اليسر إذ قتل الحمار متعمدا وهو محرم

rows.speaker: أبو حنيفة ومالك والشافعي
rows.claim: Abu Hanifa, Malik, and al-Shafi‘i treat forgetful or otherwise accidental killing like deliberate killing; deliberation means remembering ihram while intending the kill, as reported from Umar, Ibn Abbas, Tawus, al-Hasan, Ibrahim, and al-Zuhri.
rows.anchor: ومذهب أبي حنيفة ومالك والشافعي وأصحابهم أن الخطأ بنسيان أو غيره كالعمد والعمد أن يكون ذاكرا لإحرامه قاصدا للقتل

rows.speaker: الزهري
rows.claim: Al-Zuhri assigns deliberate cases to the Qur'an and mistakes or forgetfulness to the Sunna; Ibn al-Arabi approves if Sunna means the reports from Umar and Ibn Abbas.
rows.anchor: قال الزهري جزاء العمد بالقرآن والخطأ والنسيان بالسنة

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Mujahid reads “deliberately” as intending the kill while forgetting ihram; if the killer remembers ihram, the offense is too grave for expiation and invalidates pilgrimage, like invalidating prayer by speech or ritual impurity; an actual mistake incurs compensation.
rows.anchor: معناه متعمدا لقتله ناسيا لإحرامه

rows.speaker: ابن جريج
rows.claim: Ibn Jurayj reports a similar interpretation to Mujahid's distinction between forgetting ihram and knowingly violating it.
rows.anchor: وقال نحوه ابن جريج

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: A separate report from Mujahid says deliberate killing entails no compensation, only seeking God's forgiveness, and leaves pilgrimage intact.
rows.anchor: وروي عن مجاهد أنه لا جزاء عليه في قتله متعمدا ويستغفر الله وحجه تام

rows.speaker: الكوفيون
rows.claim: The Kufan readers give jazāʾ tanwin and mithlu nominative, with an omitted predicate (“there is due on him”) and mithlu adjectival to jazāʾ.
rows.anchor: وقرأ الكوفيون فجزاء بالتنوين مثل بالرفع

rows.speaker: عبد الله
rows.claim: Abd Allah reads “his recompense is like” with a pronoun referring either to the game-killer or the game; the phrase is parsed as a subject and predicate.
rows.anchor: وقرأ عبد الله فجزاؤه مثل والضمير عائد على قاتل الصيد أو على الصيد

rows.speaker: باقي السبعة
rows.claim: The other seven readers raise and annex jazāʾ to mithl; grammarians variously treat mithl as redundant or as a verbal noun annexed to its object.
rows.anchor: وقرأ باقي السبعة فجزاء مثل برفع جزاء وإضافته إلى مثل

rows.speaker: السلمي
rows.claim: Al-Sulami reads jazāʾ with nominative and tanwin, followed by mithla in the accusative, supporting the sense “a recompense matching what he killed.”
rows.anchor: قراءة السلمي فجزاء بالرفع والتنوين مثل ما قتل بالنصب

rows.speaker: محمد بن مقاتل
rows.claim: Muhammad ibn Muqatil reads jazāʾ and mithla both in the accusative, implying “let him produce a recompense like what he killed.”
rows.anchor: وقرأ محمد بن مقاتل فجزاء مثل ما قتل بنصب جزاء ومثل

rows.speaker: الحسن
rows.claim: Al-Hasan lightens the vowel in naʿam by making its ʿayn quiescent; Ibn Atiyya calls this a dialect form.
rows.anchor: وقرأ الحسن من النعم سكن العين تخفيفا كما قالوا الشعر، وقال ابن عطية هي لغة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Min al-naʿam describes the recompense, whether jazāʾ is parsed independently or annexed to mithl; Abu al-Baqa wrongly made it a circumstantial phrase describing the killed game, although livestock describes the compensation.
rows.anchor: ومن النعم صفة لجزاء سواء رفع فجزاء ومثل أو أضيف فجزاء إلى مثل

rows.speaker: الجمهور
rows.claim: The apparent likeness is similarity in species, form, and size; the majority view is attributed to Amr ibn Awf, Ibn Abbas, al-Dahhak, al-Suddi, Ibn Jubayr, Qatada, Malik, al-Shafi‘i, and Muhammad ibn al-Hasan.
rows.anchor: والظاهر في المثلية أنها مثلية في الصورة والخلقة والصغر والعظم وهو قول الجمهور

rows.speaker: النخعي وعطاء ومجاهد
rows.claim: A group of Successors, including al-Nakha‘i, Ata, and one view of Mujahid, define equivalence by value: value the game, buy food with that value, then offer it.
rows.anchor: وذهب جماعة من التابعين إلى أن المماثلة هي في القيمة يقوم الصيد المقتول ثم يشتري بقيمته طعاما

rows.speaker: أبو حنيفة وأبو يوسف
rows.claim: Abu Hanifa and Abu Yusuf let the offender use the game's value for a sacrificial animal, food for the poor, or fasting one day per half-saʿ of food.
rows.anchor: وبه قال أبو حنيفة وأبو يوسف يشتري بالقيمة هديا إن شاء وإن شاء اشترى طعاما

rows.speaker: قوم
rows.claim: Some say likeness is by form where a counterpart exists and by value where none exists; al-Razi and al-Zamakhshari argue forcefully for the Hanafi position.
rows.anchor: وقال قوم المثلية فيما وجد له مثل صورة وما لم يوجد له مثل فالمثلية في القيمة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abu Hanifa's value-based approach does not fit the verse's apparent choice among a matching livestock sacrifice, feeding the poor, or an equivalent fast.
rows.anchor: ولفظ الآية ينبو عن مذهبه إذ ظاهر الآية يقتضي التخيير بين أن يجزئ هديا من النعم مثل ما قتل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The apparent text makes compensation due only for killing, not merely capturing, eating, guiding someone to game, or wounding and reducing its value.
rows.anchor: والظاهر أن الجزاء لا يكون إلا في القتل لا في أخذ الصيد ولا في جنسه ولا في أكله

rows.speaker: أبو حنيفة
rows.claim: Abu Hanifa requires compensation for eating game; his two colleagues require only repentance because the offender merely consumed it.
rows.anchor: خلافا لأبي حنيفة إذ قال عليه جزاء ما أكل يعني قيمته وخالفه صاحباه فقالا لا شيء عليه سوى الاستغفار

rows.speaker: أبو حنيفة وأشهب
rows.claim: Abu Hanifa and Ashhab make the person who directs another to game liable; al-Shafi‘i, Malik, and Abu Thawr put liability only on the killer.
rows.anchor: خلافا لأبي حنيفة وأشهب إذ قالا يضمن الدال الجزاء

rows.speaker: المزني
rows.claim: Al-Muzani says a person who wounds game and reduces its value owes compensation; some assess the proportional loss, while Dawud owes nothing.
rows.anchor: وقال المزني عليه شيء، وقال بعض أهل العلم إذا نقص من قيمته مثلا العشر فعليه عشر قيمته، وقال داود لا شيء عليه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: When several pilgrims jointly kill one animal, the apparent ruling is one penalty because the victim is one and the killing is not attributable to every participant individually.
rows.anchor: فأما المقتول فهو واحد يجب أن يكون المثل واحد

rows.speaker: الشافعي وأحمد وإسحاق
rows.claim: Al-Shafi‘i, Ahmad, and Ishaq also impose only one penalty for a jointly killed animal; Abu Hanifa, Malik, and al-Thawri charge each participant a full penalty.
rows.anchor: وبه قال الشافعي وأحمد وإسحاق وقال أبو حنيفة ومالك والثوري يجب على كل واحد منهم جزاء واحد

rows.speaker: أبو حنيفة
rows.claim: If people outside ihram kill game inside the sanctuary, Abu Hanifa imposes one compensation; Malik requires a full penalty from each.
rows.anchor: وبه قال أبو حنيفة، وقال مالك على كل واحد جزاء كامل

rows.speaker: أبو يوسف ومحمد
rows.claim: Because the verse states livestock without an age condition, Abu Yusuf and Muhammad allow a young male or female goat proportionate to the game.
rows.anchor: وظاهر قوله من النعم أنه لا يشترط سن فيجزئ الجفر والعناق على قدر الصيد وبه قال أبو يوسف ومحمد

rows.speaker: أبو حنيفة
rows.claim: Abu Hanifa requires a sacrificial animal of the age valid for the ritual sacrifice or the combined Hajj-and-Umra offering.
rows.anchor: وقال أبو حنيفة لا يجوز أن يهدي إلا ما يجزئ في الأضحية وهدي القران

rows.speaker: الشافعي
rows.claim: Al-Shafi‘i holds that a person who hunts lawfully outside the sanctuary and then slaughters the game inside it owes no penalty and may eat it; Abu Hanifa requires compensation.
rows.anchor: أنه لو صاد الحلال بالحل ثم ذبحه في الحرم فلا ضمان وهو حلال وبه قال الشافعي، وقال أبو حنيفة عليه الجزاء

rows.speaker: ابن وهب
rows.claim: Ibn Wahb says the two judges let the killer choose among sacrifice, feeding, and fasting; they assess a sheep when appropriate, otherwise food, with a day of fasting per mudd; Malik agrees.
rows.anchor: قال ابن وهب من السنة أن يخير الحكمان من قتل الصيد كما خيره الله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The two judges are apparently two just men, not two women; Umar used Abd al-Rahman ibn Awf to judge a gazelle as a sheep, as did Jarir and Ibn Umar.
rows.anchor: والظاهر أن العدلين ذكران فلا يحكم فيه امرأتان عدلتان

rows.speaker: جعفر بن محمد
rows.claim: Jaʿfar ibn Muhammad reads the verb in the singular, meaning a person of justice among you, without intending that only one judge act.
rows.anchor: وقرأ جعفر بن محمد يحكم به ذوا عدل على التوحيد أي يحكم به من يعدل منكم

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: Another interpretation takes the judge as the ruler or imam.
rows.anchor: وقيل أراد به الإمام

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The judges apparently use independent reasoning; Abu Hanifa, Malik, and other scholars agree. Al-Shafi‘i follows Companion rulings where available, then chooses the closest of the three livestock kinds.
rows.anchor: والظاهر أن الحكمين يحكمان في جزاء الصيد باجتهادهما وذلك موكول إليهما

rows.speaker: مالك
rows.claim: Malik says neither judge may be the game-killer; al-Shafi‘i permits an accidental killer to serve, but not a deliberate killer, who sins by the act.
rows.anchor: والظاهر أن الحكمين لا يكون أحدهما قاتل الصيد وهو قول مالك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The requirement that two judges determine the counterpart by judgment supports the legitimacy of analogical reasoning.
rows.anchor: واستدل بقوله تعالى: يحكم به ذوا عدل منكم على إثبات القياس

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The grammar permits hadyan as a circumstantial phrase describing the recompense, an apposition to mithl, or a source-accusative; most plausibly it describes “by it.”
rows.anchor: وجوزوا في انتصاب قوله هديا أن يكون حالا من فجزاء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Balighan al-Kaʿba means the sacrifice is slaughtered within the sanctuary: Abu Hanifa allows anywhere in it, while al-Shafi‘i specifies the Kaʿba precinct; marked offerings go to Mina, others to Mecca or the sanctuary after entering from outside it.
rows.anchor: ومعنى بالغ الكعبة أن ينحر بالحرم ويتصدق به حيث شاء عند أبي حنيفة، وقال الشافعي بالحرم،

rows.speaker: الأعرج
rows.claim: Al-Aʿraj reads hadyan with kasra on dal and a doubled ya.
rows.anchor: وقرأ الأعرج هديا بكسر الدال وتشديد الياء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The phrase min-kum indicates that the two judges must be Muslims.
rows.anchor: وفي قوله منكم دليل على أنهما من المسلمين

rows.speaker: الصاحبان
rows.claim: The two Kufan companions read “or expiation of food for the poor” by annexing expiation to food; al-Farisi objects that expiation is for killing game, not for food, but the author permits a loose annexation.
rows.anchor: قرأ الصاحبان بالإضافة والإضافة تكون بأدنى ملابسة

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhshari takes the annexation as “expiation from food,” like a ring of silver; the author rejects this because food is not the genus of expiation except by an excessively remote metaphor.
rows.anchor: وأما ما ذهب إليه الزمخشري من زعمه أن الإضافة مبينة كأنه قيل أو كفارة من طعام مساكين

rows.speaker: باقي السبعة
rows.claim: The other seven readers use tanwin and nominative taʿam; al-Aʿraj and Isa ibn Umar do likewise but use singular miskin as a collective noun. Abu Ali calls taʿam apposition, though the author prefers parsing it as a substitute.
rows.anchor: وقرأ باقي السبعة بالتنوين ورفع طعام وقرأ كذلك الأعرج وعيسى بن عمر إلا أنهما أفردا مسكين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse leaves the amount of food and number of poor unspecified; apparently the minimum plural “poor” suffices.
rows.anchor: وقد أجمل في مقدار الطعام وفي عدد المساكين والظاهر أنه يكفي أقل ما ينطلق عليه جمع مساكين

rows.speaker: إبراهيم وعطاء ومجاهد والقاسم
rows.claim: Ibrahim, Ata, Mujahid, and al-Qasim value the game in cash and buy food, giving each poor person half a saʿ; this valuation is also reported from Ibn Abbas and adopted by Abu Hanifa.
rows.anchor: وقال إبراهيم وعطاء ومجاهد والقاسم يقوم الصيد دراهم ثم يشتري بالدراهم طعاما فيطعم كل مسكين نصف صاع

rows.speaker: مجاهد وعطاء وابن عباس والشافعي وأحمد
rows.claim: Mujahid, Ata, Ibn Abbas, al-Shafi‘i, and Ahmad value the sacrificial animal, then buy food for that amount.
rows.anchor: وقال مجاهد وعطاء وابن عباس والشافعي وأحمد يقوم الهدي ثم يشتري بقيمة الهدي طعاما

rows.speaker: مالك
rows.claim: Malik's preferred method values the game, buys the equivalent food, feeds each poor person one mudd, and fasts one day for each mudd.
rows.anchor: وقال مالك أحسن ما سمعت، أنه يقوم الصيد فينظركم ثمنه من الطعام فيطعم لكل مسكين مدا ويصوم مكان كل مد يوما

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “That” most likely refers to the nearest antecedent, food; because its amount is unspecified, the required number of fasting days is also unspecified and follows the dispute over one or two mudds.
rows.anchor: الأظهر أن يكون ذلك إشارة إلى أقرب مذكور وهو الطعام والطعام المذكور غير معين في الآية

rows.speaker: ابن عباس ومالك
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas and Malik calculate one fasting day per mudd of food; al-Shafi‘i uses two mudds, and Ahmad transmits both positions.
rows.anchor: وبالمد قال ابن عباس ومالك، وبالمدين قال الشافعي وعن أحمد القولان

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: If “that” instead refers to the animal killed, Ibn Abbas assigns three days for a gazelle, twenty for a camel, and thirty for an ostrich or wild donkey.
rows.anchor: وجوزوا أن يكون ذلك إشارة إلى الصيد المقتول وفي الظبي ثلاثة أيام وفي الإبل عشرون يوما

rows.speaker: ابن جبير
rows.claim: Ibn Jubayr gives a range of three to ten fasting days under the animal-based interpretation.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن جبير ثلاثة أيام إلى عشرة أيام

rows.speaker: جماعة من العلماء
rows.claim: A group of scholars imposes no location restriction on feeding or fasting; Ata and others require sacrifice and feeding in Mecca but allow fasting anywhere.
rows.anchor: والظاهر عدم تقييد الإطعام والصوم بمكان وبه قال جماعة من العلماء

rows.speaker: الجمهور
rows.claim: The majority read ʿadl with fatḥa on the ʿayn; Ibn Abbas, Talha ibn Musarrif, and al-Jahdari read it with kasra, a word explained earlier in al-Baqara.
rows.anchor: وقرأ الجمهور أو عدل بفتح العين، وقرأ ابن عباس وطلحة بن مصرف والجحدري بكسرها

rows.speaker: الجمهور
rows.claim: The apparent force of “or” is a choice among the three options, whether the offender is wealthy or poor; Ibn Abbas, Ibrahim, and Hammad ibn Salama require moving to food or fasting only when unable to offer the preceding option.
rows.anchor: والظاهر أن أو للتخيير أي ذلك فعل أجزأه موسرا كان أو معسرا

rows.speaker: الجمهور
rows.claim: The apparent choice belongs to the game-killer; Muhammad ibn al-Hasan instead gives the choice to the two judges.
rows.anchor: والظاهر أن التخيير راجع إلى قاتل الصيد وهو قول الجمهور

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The apparent duty is one of the three alternatives, without combining feeding and fasting in one expiation; Abu Hanifa's followers permit combining them.
rows.anchor: والظاهر أن الواجب أحد هذه الثلاثة فلا يجمع بين الإطعام والصيام

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The accusative siyāman is a specification of the equivalent amount, meaning “or an equivalent amount in fasting.”
rows.anchor: وانتصب صياما على التمييز على العدل

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhshari connects li-yadhuqa to jazāʾ, construing the sentence as “he must compensate or expiate so that he tastes” the consequences.
rows.anchor: قال الزمخشري ليذوق متعلق بقوله فجزاء أي فعليه أن يجازى أو يكفر ليذوق

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: That attachment fails on the reading with tanwin and nominative mithl; there the source noun is adjectivally qualified, so the phrase instead depends on an omitted verb, “he was recompensed thereby so that he might taste.”
rows.anchor: والصواب أن تتعلق هذه القراءة بفعل محذوف التقدير جوزي بذلك ليذوق

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Some grammarians wrongly attach li-yadhuqa to ʿadlu dhālika.
rows.anchor: ووقع لبعض المعربين أنها تتعلق بعدل ذلك وهو غلط

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Taste” is metaphorical for the cost and bodily hardship of fasting; wabāl is the bad consequence of violating ihram's sanctity by killing game.
rows.anchor: واستعير هنا لما يؤثر من غرامة وإتعاب النفس بالصوم والوبال سوء عاقبة ما فعل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “God pardoned what is past” refers to pre-Islamic killing of game in the sanctuary.
rows.anchor: عفا الله عما سلف أي في جاهليتكم من قتلكم الصيد في الحرم

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhshari explains the pardon by saying the community followed earlier revealed laws that already prohibited hunting.
rows.anchor: قال الزمخشري: لأنهم كانوا متعبدين بشرائع من قبلهم، وكان الصيد فيها محرما

rows.speaker: ابن زيد
rows.claim: Ibn Zayd takes “what is past” as believers' killing of game before this prohibition was revealed.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن زيد: عما سلف لكم أيها المؤمنون من قتل الصيد قبل هذا النهي والتحريم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: On one interpretation of a return to killing game, one who deems it lawful faces punishment in the afterlife; one who forgets ihram expiates by one of the three alternatives.
rows.anchor: فإن كان مستحلا فينتقم الله منه في الآخرة ويكفر أو ناسيا لإحرامه كفر بإحدى الخصال الثلاث

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas says a deliberate, knowledgeable repeat offender owes no expiation and is punished by God; Shurayh, al-Nakha‘i, al-Hasan, Mujahid, Ibn Zayd, and Dawud agree.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن عباس: إن كان متعمدا عالما بإحرامه فلا كفارة عليه وينتقم الله منه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The conditional wording “whoever returns” is general, contrary to those who restrict it to one named person; even if the report of a man burned after a second offense is sound, he is only one instance of the general rule.
rows.anchor: وظاهر ومن عاد للعموم ألا ترى أن من شرطية أو موصولة تضمنت معنى الشرط فتعم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The fāʾ in “then God takes vengeance” answers the conditional or the relative pronoun understood conditionally, with an implied subject in the latter parse.
rows.anchor: والفاء في فينتقم جواب الشرط أو الداخلة على الموصول المضمن معنى الشرط

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Mighty, Lord of vengeance” means no one can overcome God when He wills to punish; the close is a reminder of punishment and a threat.
rows.anchor: أي عزيز لا يغالب إذا أراد أن ينتقم لم يغالبه أحد

rows.speaker: الكلبي
rows.claim: Al-Kalbi says the sea-game verse was revealed when Banu Mudlij, living on the coast, asked about fish stranded by receding water.
rows.anchor: قال الكلبي: نزلت في بني مدلج وكانوا ينزلون في أسياف البحر سألوا عما نضب عنه الماء من السمك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The apparent broad meaning of sea is any abundant water, including rivers, valleys, ponds, springs, and seas, with no difference in the ruling; another view restricts it to the great sea based on the revelation occasion.
rows.anchor: والبحر هنا الماء الكثير الواسع وسواء في ذلك النهر والوادي والبركة والعين لا يختلف الحكم في ذلك

rows.speaker: أبو بكر وعمر وابن عمر
rows.claim: Abu Bakr, Umar, and Ibn Umar take “its food” to mean what the sea casts out and what floats on it.
rows.anchor: وأما طعامه فروي عن أبي بكر وعمر وابن عمر أنه ما قذفه البحر وطفا عليه

rows.speaker: قتادة وابن جبير والنخعي وابن المسيب ومجاهد والسدي
rows.claim: Qatada, Ibn Jubayr, al-Nakha‘i, Ibn al-Musayyib, Mujahid, and al-Suddi say sea-game is fresh and its food is salted fish; this is also reported from Ibn Abbas and Zayd ibn Thabit.
rows.anchor: وقال قتادة وابن جبير والنخعي وابن المسيب ومجاهد والسدي صيده طريه وطعامه المملوح منه

rows.speaker: أبو عبد الله
rows.claim: Abu Abd Allah calls the fresh-versus-salted interpretation weak because salted fish was fresh game at first, making the distinction repetitive.
rows.anchor: قال أبو عبد الله وهذا ضعيف لأن الذي صار مالحا قد كان طريا وصيدا في أول الأمر

rows.speaker: قوم
rows.claim: Some interpret sea-food as salt crystallized from its water, along with its plants and similar things.
rows.anchor: وقال قوم: طعامه الملح الذي ينعقد من مائه وسائر ما فيه من نبات ونحوه

rows.speaker: الحسن
rows.claim: Al-Hasan interprets its food as what the sea throws onto its shore.
rows.anchor: وقال الحسن: طعامه صوب ساحله

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: Another view calls anything nourished by seawater its food, because it grows from that water.
rows.anchor: وقيل: طعامه كل ما سقاه الماء فأنبت لأنه نبت من ماء البحر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Sea-game can include creatures hunted for purposes other than eating, such as shells for pearls or animals for bones and teeth; “its food” then specifies edible things, while the unrestricted permission covers pilgrims and non-pilgrims.
rows.anchor: وقيل: صيد البحر ما صيد لأكل وغيره كالصدف لأجل اللؤلؤ وبعض الحيوانات لأجل عظامها وأسنانها

rows.speaker: ابن أبي ليلى ومالك والأوزاعي
rows.claim: Ibn Abi Layla, Malik, and al-Awza‘i apparently permit eating every sea creature, including water-pig, water-dog, water-snake, crab, and frog.
rows.anchor: والظاهر أنه يحل أكل كل ما صيد من أنواع مخلوقاته حتى الذي يسمى خنزير الماء وكلب الماء

rows.speaker: الليث
rows.claim: Al-Layth forbids water-pig and water-human but permits eating sea carrion, dog, and horse.
rows.anchor: وقال الليث: لا يؤكل خنزير الماء ولا إنسان الماء وتؤكل ميتته وكلبه وفرسه

rows.speaker: أبو حنيفة والثوري
rows.claim: Abu Hanifa and al-Thawri allow only fish among aquatic animals, excluding floating fish, frogs, water-dogs, and water-pigs as unclean.
rows.anchor: وقال أبو حنيفة والثوري فيما روى عنه أبو إسحاق الفزاري لا يؤكل من حيوان الماء إلا السمك

rows.speaker: الرازي
rows.claim: Al-Razi permits all kinds of fish but prohibits frogs; the scholars differ over the remaining creatures.
rows.anchor: قال الرازي: ما صيد من البحر حيتان وجميع أنواعها حلال وضفادع وجميع أنواعها حرام

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhshari reads sea-game as all hunted sea creatures and its food as edible prey: Abu Hanifa limits food to fish, while Ibn Abi Layla permits all hunted creatures; the author says “that you eat it” is less apparent than taking the pronoun as the sea and food as edible things.
rows.anchor: وطعامه بقوله وأن تطعموه خلاف الظاهر ويكون على قول ابن أبي ليلى الضمير عائدا على صيد البحر

rows.speaker: ابن عباس وعبد الله بن الحارث
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas and Abd Allah ibn al-Harith read ṭaʿmihi, “its food,” supporting the meaning of edible food rather than the act of feeding.
rows.anchor: وقراءة ابن عباس وعبد الله بن الحارث وطعمه بضم الطاء وسكون العين

rows.speaker: ابن عطية
rows.claim: Ibn Atiyya parses mutāʿan as a cognate accusative, meaning that God grants a benefit by it.
rows.anchor: وانتصب متاعا قال ابن عطية على المصدر والمعنى متعكم به متاعا

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhshari parses mutāʿan as purpose: the sea's food is granted as enjoyment, eaten fresh by residents and preserved as provisions by travelers, like Moses provisioning on his journey to al-Khidr.
rows.anchor: وقال الزمخشري متاعا لكم مفعول له أي أحل لكم تمتيعا لكم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhshari's food-only purpose rests on the Hanafi distinction between edible food and other sea-game; on other schools the purpose can concern both game and food.
rows.anchor: وتخصيصه المفعول له بقوله: وطعاما جار على مذهبه مذهب أبي حنيفة

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Mujahid takes “you” as coastal villagers and “travelers” as city-dwellers who bring provisions inland; the disagreement concerns residents versus travelers and fresh versus salted fish.
rows.anchor: وقال مجاهد: الخطاب لأهل القرى والسيارة، أهل الأمصار

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The closing command to fear God is a warning after lawful and forbidden matters; mentioning the gathering reminds people that obedience and disobedience will be made manifest there.
rows.anchor: واتقوا الله الذي إليه تحشرون هذا فيه تنبيه وتهديد وجاء عقيب تحليل وتحريم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: After describing how God destroys sinners, the passage has the Prophet ask who owns the heavens and earth: the answer must be God, proving Him their owner and the one who destroys them for sin; the question rebukes and elicits acknowledgment.
rows.anchor: لما ذكر تعالى تصريفه فيمن أهلكهم بذنوبهم، أمر نبيه صلى الله عليه وسلم بسؤالهم ذلك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The command also makes the Prophet himself first acknowledge that ownership belongs to God.
rows.anchor: ثم أمره تعالى بنسبة ذلك لله تعالى ليكون أول من بادر إلى الاعتراف بذلك

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: One grammatical reading supplies an omitted exchange: if they do not answer, say, “It belongs to God.”
rows.anchor: وقيل: في الكلام حذف تقديره فإذا لم يجيبوا قل لله

rows.speaker: قوم
rows.claim: Others understand the people to have failed to answer, after which they are told to say “God's”; li-llāh is a predicate of an omitted subject.
rows.anchor: وقال قوم: المعنى أنه أمر بالسؤال فكأنه لما لم يجيبوا سألوا فقيل لهم قل لله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: After asserting that God created and governs the world by His will, the verse follows with mercy and beneficence; kataba apparently means literally “wrote.”
rows.anchor: لما ذكر تعالى أنه موجد العالم المتصرف فيهم بما يريد، ودل ذلك على نفاذ قدرته أردفه بذكر رحمته

rows.speaker: قوم
rows.claim: Some take “wrote” literally: God commanded that mercy be inscribed in the Preserved Tablet.
rows.anchor: وقال به قوم هنا وله أريد حقيقة الكتب والمعنى أمر بالكتب في اللوح المحفوظ

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: Other explanations take “wrote” to mean promised, informed, graciously made binding without an obligation imposed on God, or decreed and carried out.
rows.anchor: وقيل: كتب هنا بمعنى وعد بها فضلا وكرما. وقيل: بمعنى أخبر. وقيل: أوجب إيجاب فضل وكرم

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhshari says God imposed mercy on Himself by guiding people to know Him and presenting proofs of His oneness in the creation they already acknowledge.
rows.anchor: وقال الزمخشري: أي أوجبها على ذاته في هدايتكم إلى معرفته

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Mercy apparently means God's general kindness to both good and bad people in this world; because no recipient is specified, it is general.
rows.anchor: والرحمة هنا الظاهر أنها عامة فتعم المحسن والمسيء في الدنيا

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: Another view treats the definite article as referring to the one mercy sent from the hundred created mercies, with ninety-nine reserved for the afterlife.
rows.anchor: وقيل: الألف واللام للعهد، فيراد بها الرحمة الواحدة التي أنزلها الله تعالى من المائة الرحمة

rows.speaker: الزجاج
rows.claim: Al-Zajjaj says mercy here means giving disbelievers time and longer lives to repent rather than punishing them immediately.
rows.anchor: وقال الزجاج: الرحمة إمهال الكفار وتعميرهم ليتوبوا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A report in Sahih Muslim says that after creating creation, God wrote in a book kept with Him: “My mercy overcomes My anger.”
rows.anchor: وفي صحيح مسلم لما قضى الله الخلق كتب في كتاب على نفسه، فهو موضوع عنده إن رحمتي تغلب غضبي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: After mentioning mercy, the verse mentions resurrection and recompense for good and evil; the oath-like clause is syntactically independent of the preceding words but related in meaning.
rows.anchor: لما ذكر أنه تعالى رحم عباده ذكر الحشر وأن فيه المجازاة على الخير والشر

rows.speaker: المهدوي
rows.claim: Al-Mahdawi reports grammarians who read “He will surely gather you” as an explanation of mercy (“that He gather you”), a clause in the accusative as an apposition.
rows.anchor: وحكى المهدوي أن جماعة من النحويين قالوا: إنها تفسير للرحمة تقديره: أن يجمعكم

rows.speaker: ابن عطية
rows.claim: Ibn Atiyya rejects the apposition analysis, arguing that the emphatic nūn enters commands, prohibitions, and expressions restricted by an oath.
rows.anchor: ورد ذلك ابن عطية بأن النون الثقيلة تكون قد دخلت في الإيجاب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author says Ibn Atiyya's limits on emphatic nūn are too narrow: it occurs in conditional clauses such as “if Satan incites you,” and oath constructions have grammatical conditions; the gathered sentence can resemble an oath despite its non-oath meaning.
rows.anchor: وهذا الذي ذكره لا يحصر مواضع دخول نون التوكيد، ألا ترى دخولها في الشرط

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author further argues that an oath's sworn clause has no syntactic position by itself, although an oath construction can occupy a position when embedded in a sentence.
rows.anchor: أن الجملة المقسم عليها لا موضع لها وحدها من الإعراب

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: One reading takes the gathering literally as assembling people in their graves until Resurrection; apparently ilā marks the endpoint. Another takes it as creating successive generations in this world until then.
rows.anchor: والجمع هنا قيل حقيقة أي ليجمعنكم في القبور إلى يوم القيامة

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: Some take ilā as “for,” as in the verse “You will gather the people for a day in which there is no doubt”; readings that make it “in” or an extra particle are judged remote.
rows.anchor: وقد تكون إلى هنا بمعنى اللام أي ليوم القيامة، كقوله تعالى: إنك جامع الناس ليوم لا ريب فيه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The pronoun in “there is no doubt in it” apparently refers to the Day of Resurrection, rebutting those who doubt it, though it may instead refer to the gathering itself.
rows.anchor: والظاهر أن الضمير في فيه عائد إلى يوم القيامة وفيه رد على من ارتاب في الحشر

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: A further view restricts this mercy to those who believe and affirm the messengers.
rows.anchor: الرحمة لمن آمن وصدق الرسل
